Vignette:
# Amira's Case

Amira was fifty-nine when she came to the clinic on a gray November afternoon, her posture rigid in the waiting room chair. She had been a police officer for thirty-two years—most of her adult life spent in a uniform, trained to notice threats, to stay alert, to protect. That training had saved her life once. It could not save her the second time.

Three years ago, on a routine call to a domestic disturbance in a neighborhood she had patrolled for two decades, Amira had been ambushed by the ex-partner of the woman she was trying to help. He had been waiting behind the kitchen door with a length of pipe. The first blow had caught her across the ribs. The second had been aimed at her head but she had turned, and it had landed on her shoulder instead. She remembered the sound of his breathing—ragged, furious—and the sound of the pipe itself, the whistle it made through the air before impact. She remembered the woman screaming. She remembered, with absolute clarity, the moment she realized her training meant nothing, that her badge meant nothing, that she could not control what was happening to her body.

The man had been arrested. He had served fourteen months. He was out now. Amira had come to believe that the system had failed her, that what had happened was not merely a crime but a profound injustice—one that had been compounded by his early release, by the way the case had moved through the courts, by the way her own department had handled her return to duty. Nothing had been done about it in any way that mattered. The unfairness of it lived in her like a stone.

For the first year after the assault, Amira had tried to return to work. But something had shifted in her body's relationship to the world. When she was driving with other officers in the patrol car, her heart would begin to race without warning—a pounding so forceful she could feel it in her throat, in her temples. The sensation terrified her more than the assault itself sometimes did, because it meant her body was betraying her, reacting as if danger were present when she was sitting in a vehicle with trained colleagues in broad daylight. She had come to believe that her own physiology had become an enemy, that it could turn on her at any moment and she would be helpless to stop it.

The memories themselves were vivid and intrusive. When they came—often without trigger, sometimes in the middle of the night—she did not simply recall the event. She heard the sounds again: the whistle of the pipe, the woman's screams, the man's breathing. The terror that flooded through her was the same terror from that moment, undiluted by time. Her therapist in those early months had called it re-experiencing. Amira called it being trapped.

By the second year, she had stopped driving with her partner. She had requested desk duty. Then she had taken medical leave. Then, gradually, she had begun to withdraw from everyone. Her sister called; Amira did not answer. Her husband, Khalil, would sit in the living room in the evenings, and Amira would retreat to the bedroom, not because she was angry with him but because she could not bear the weight of his presence, his concern, his inability to fix what had been broken. She had come to believe that she could not rely on other people—not because they were malicious, but because reliance itself was a vulnerability she could no longer afford. Her friends from the department stopped trying to visit. Her extended family stopped calling. The isolation had accumulated so gradually that by the time she recognized it, she had already cut herself off almost completely.

What frightened her most now, in the quiet of her isolation, was the thought that she was going crazy. She monitored her own mind constantly, watching for signs of deterioration, interpreting her intrusive thoughts as evidence of mental breakdown. She was hypervigilant not only for dangerous people in the world but for danger within herself—for the moment when her mind might fracture entirely.

It was Khalil who finally insisted she come. He had found her one afternoon sitting in the dark, unable to articulate why, and he had said, with the exhaustion of someone who loves a person they cannot reach: "We need help. Please."
